question: to the Commission Aura Salla (PPE), Mika Aaltola (PPE), Pekka Toveri (PPE), Alexandra Mehnert (PPE), Andrea Wechsler (PPE), Maria Guzenina (S&D), Maria Grapini (S&D), Lucia Yar (Renew), Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Per Clausen (The Left), Merja Kyllönen (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Sirpa Pietikäinen (PPE), Wouter Beke (PPE), Axel Voss (PPE), Michael McNamara (Renew), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Emil Radev (PPE) Subject:

A recent ruling by the Supreme Court of the United States weakens the independence of key federal oversight bodies and may undermine the legal assumptions underpinning the EU–US Data Privacy Framework. As the stability of transatlantic data transfers depends on effective and independent oversight in the United States, this development highlights the EU’s continued exposure to external legal and political developments and the need to strengthen European digital sovereignty. Considering this: 1.
Will the Commission urgently assess the implications of the ruling for the validity and stability of the EU–US Data Privacy Framework?
What steps is the Commission taking to strengthen European data sovereignty and reduce the EU’s dependence on non-EU data transfer mechanisms?
Is the Commission preparing contingency measures, including an orderly transition, should the current framework become legally unsustainable?
answer: (English version) to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (25 June 2026) Subject: EU-US biometric data-sharing agreement and US data protection practice Negotiations between the EU and the United States on the framework agreement regarding the exchange of personal data, including biometric data, for the purpose of screening and identity verification of travellers (1), are expected to be concluded soon. According to the Commission, in this context ‘ensur[ing] respect of the EU’s standards on the protection of personal data’ is a ‘key priority’ (2). This should not only be the case prior to signing an agreement, but also afterwards, in practice. The EU-US Umbrella Agreement, in force since 2017 and intended to improve the overall level of data protection in EU-US law enforcement cooperation, was supposed to be jointly reviewed by 2020. However, six years later, a joint review report has yet to be published. 1. Why was no joint review of the EU-US Umbrella Agreement published, despite the legal requirement to do so (3)? If the data protection requirements of that agreement cannot be reviewed or assessed because there are no results to review, and noting the worrying developments in the US regarding the protection of personal data, how does the Commission expect EU citizens to have trust in the US authorities as regards the safety of their transferred biometric data? 2. Will the Commission ensure that the draft agreement fully incorporates the standards set by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in relevant case law (4), and if so, is it convinced that the envisaged agreement would hold up in court? Priority question for written answer P-002741/26 to the Commission Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew) (2 July 2026) Subject: Validity of EU-US Data Privacy Framework following US Supreme Court judgment In 2023, the Commission issued an adequacy decision in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for data transfers to the United States, implemented under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. In this adequacy decision, the Commission relied on the US Federal Trade Commission as an ‘independent’ supervisory authority with the power to monitor and enforce compliance with the data protection rules (1). On 29 June 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that independent executive authorities in the United States are unconstitutional (2), which raises questions regarding the validity of the Commission’s adequacy decision, leaving both citizens and companies in legal uncertainty. In 2015 and 2020, earlier adequacy decisions for data transfers to the US were invalidated by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), because of a lack of adequate data protection in the United States.

to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) (13 July 2026) Subject: Urgent need to develop European cloud service providers The US Supreme Court has paved the way for the President of the United States to dismiss the commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission, the agency responsible, amongst other things, for protecting the personal data of Europeans when it is processed by US tech firms (1). Since 1935, the independence of these commissioners had been based on protection against politically-motivated dismissal: the President of the United States could appoint them, but could not remove them from office. The US Supreme Court has now made such removal possible which, in turn, runs counter to the data transfer agreement, concluded by the European Union with the United States, and known as the ‘Data Privacy Framework’. This agreement was in fact conditional upon the existence of independent supervisory authorities in the United States. Does the Commission plan to renegotiate the data transfer agreement with the United States, given that the legal challenges already brought before the Court of Justice of the European Union have a strong chance of success?
